statement: This method is based on the reaction of absorbed O2 with Na2SO3. Copper and cobalt ions can be used as catalyst.

Mostly, there is a concentration range in which the reaction proceeds so rapidly that the dissolved oxygen concentration in the liquid is nil. This implies that the reaction largely takes place in the boundary layer and that the driving force is larger than if there were only physically controlled absorption. The apparent kLA thus determined should then be converted into the kLA for that absorption.
The conversion makes it necessary to determine both the reaction rate constant kR and the order of the reaction, and, as appears from the literature, problems arise here.
Onken and Schalk (1977) have demonstrated that the addition of 5% glycerin reduces kR by a factor of 25.
The order of the reaction in oxygen may vary from 1 at a partial pressure of 1 atm to 2 at low partial pressures, as demonstrated by Reith and Beek (1973).
An additional problem is that for the sulfite technique to be successful, high ionic concentrations (1 to 2 M) are required.
In most cases, the sulfite method utilizes 10-100 g of sulfite/L, which implies a high ion concentration. Therefore, the results obtained by this method are included in this section.
